title: A hymn in Sri Rag
hook: the four watches of the night picture a life from birth to old age (Sri Rag M1, ang 74)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sri Rag, grave and slow, the best raga if it brings love of the True One. Your line was the first raga.

Vanjaariaa mitraa. O merchant friend. Those words run through a hymn of Guru Nanak in Sri Rag, on ang seventy-four: they open every stanza and come again inside it, so a singer keeps returning to them. Earlier on the path you read this hymn closely, the four watches of the night laid over a single life. Today the same hymn, heard the way it was written to be heard: sung, slowly, in yesterday's grave evening raga.
screen: `O MERCHANT FRIEND.` → `THE FOUR WATCHES, AGAIN.` → `THIS TIME, SUNG.`

segments.voice: On the page, the hymn is a map. In the first watch of the night, by command a life is placed in the womb. In the second, the child is carried and adored. In the third, the mind turns to wealth and youth. In the fourth, the reaper comes to the field. Each stanza closes with Guru Nanak's name and a word to the mortal in that watch. Now hear it in Sri Rag. The raga is slow and grave, and its mood holds from stanza to stanza while the life inside it moves: womb, childhood, the busy middle, the last cold stretch. A whole night goes by in a few minutes of singing, and the music never hurries. That steadiness does something the page can't: it makes the listener sit through each watch at the same pace, the bright ones and the hard ones alike. And in every stanza the call comes back. Merchant friend. A trader is someone sent out with capital, expected to come back with something to show. A friend is someone who tells you the truth while there's still time to act on it. Sung again and again, the call stops being a label and becomes a voice at the door, knocking in each watch. So the question the hymn leaves is quieter and more present than which watch a life is in. Right now, in this hour, which watch is it? Tomorrow the music changes, to a raga from the Punjab's own soil.
screen: `FOUR WATCHES, ONE LIFE.` · `THE TUNE HOLDS STEADY AS LIFE MOVES.` · `THE CALL RETURNS IN EVERY STANZA.` · then, large: `WHICH WATCH NOW.`

segments.voice: If you can find this hymn, the pehre of Guru Nanak in Sri Rag, let it play while you sit; if not, say the call softly once, vanjaariaa mitraa, and sit in the quiet it leaves. Don't add up your whole life; just ask about this hour, whether it's a beginning, a being-carried, a building or a settling of accounts, and let the answer be small and honest. If you pray, answer the friend's call with one Waheguru.
A hymn in Sri Rag. Guru Nanak's four watches of the night, sung in a slow, grave raga that holds steady while a life moves through it, with the merchant friend called in every stanza. Today's word.
screen: `A HYMN IN SRI RAG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: which watch now. The merchant friend is called again in every stanza. Rest well.

howItsDone: Guru Nanak's pehre are sung in Sri Rag in kirtan, and Sikhs also read them in the Guru Granth Sahib as a reflection on the stages of a life.

what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak's pehre in Sri Rag (Ang 74) carry the address vanjaariaa mitraa in the first line of every stanza and again within it, and close each stanza with his name, so the form itself, sung in Sri Rag, turns the call into a refrain across the four watches.

chat.says: Why does that Sri Rag hymn keep calling out 'merchant friend'?
options: It's a voice at the door in each watch, asking what you'll bring back while there's time.
It's just a rhyme to fill out the tune; the words don't matter when it's sung.
It's a warning that earning money is wrong at every stage of a life.
chat.meaning: The call returns in every stanza. A trader is sent out to come back with something to show; a friend tells the truth while there's still time.
